To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Black college experience does not have a positive effect on Black students' psychological development.

African-American students attending historically black institutions of higher education are significantly more advanced in their psychosocial development than African-American students attending predominantly white institutions of higher education.

African American college students in predominantly Black institutions are not more likely than their counterparts in predominantly White institutions to be at a higher level of psychosocial development or to have a stronger ethnic identity or to be more likely to choose a career in an area of high demand.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the psychosocial and intellectual development of African-American students attending historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs) and predominantly white institutions (PWIs)
the effects of institutional type on the development of African-American students.

the Black student's psychosocial development is enhanced when the college he attends has a Black student body and faculty, and when the college is located in the Black community.

, while it is not possible to generalize that the psychosocial and academic development of African-American students is better assured by Black institutions than by White institutions, there does exist a significant difference between the two types of institutions in the development of the students' ethnic identity and career choice, and in the students' lifestyle.
